title: Coil-built frog planter
subtitle: A small smiling frog figure that holds a succulent or tiny plant, no kiln needed
excerpt: A frog planter combines a coil-built bowl body with a pinch-built head and four flat legs. The bowl interior holds a small pot or a little soil for a succulent. Made in air-dry clay and sealed with waterproof varnish, it sits on a windowsill or shelf.
sourceNotes: Animal planter forms derived from first principles. Air-dry clay construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A roll of clay used as the building unit in coil construction; joined and smoothed to build up vessel walls
Roughening both surfaces and applying clay diluted with water before pressing pieces together
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but is still damp enough to trim and join additional pieces

content.text: A frog planter is a
coil

-built bowl, about 10 cm across, with a frog head and legs attached at leather-hard stage. The bowl interior is the planting space. An air-dry clay frog sits on a table or windowsill; once sealed with waterproof varnish, it tolerates occasional light watering from a small plant pot inside.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay thinned with water)

content.text: Building the bowl body
Roll a base circle 10 cm in diameter, 7 mm thick. Set it flat on a board.
Roll four coils, each about 1 cm diameter and 35 cm long. Add coils around the base perimeter one at a time, blending each into the previous layer with a wooden rib on the inside and outside.
After the fourth coil the bowl should be about 5 cm tall. Smooth the walls to 6 mm thickness. The top rim should be wide enough to hold a 7-8 cm plant pot or small handful of soil.
Making the head
Roll 80 g of clay into a slightly flattened ball, about 6 cm wide and 4 cm tall. This is the head.
Press two small ball eyes , 1.5 cm diameter , and
Score the eyes and the top of the head, apply slip, and press the eyes onto the head. Blend the join at the base of each eye.
Use a needle tool to draw a wide smile curved slightly upward on the front lower face of the head. Press a small flat oval of clay above the smile for a snout.
Making the legs and attaching
Roll four flat oval legs from small portions of clay. Front legs: 5 cm long, 2 cm wide. Rear legs: 6 cm long with a bent knee shape. Use a needle to score toe lines on each foot end.
Allow the bowl and head to reach
Use the
score-and-slip
method to attach the head to the front of the bowl rim. Support the head from underneath with a small ball of scrap clay while the joint firms.
Attach the front legs to the bowl sides below the head. Attach the rear legs to the back of the bowl, angling outward and slightly backward.
Drying, painting, and sealing
Dry the frog on its back legs and base for two to three days, covering loosely with a cloth for the first day. Once
leather-hard

then fully dry, paint with bright green acrylic, adding yellow-green highlights on the back and around the eyes. Add white highlight dots to each eye and a black pupil. Seal with at least two coats of waterproof acrylic varnish inside and out to make the bowl water-resistant.
Variations
Build a matching lily-pad saucer by pressing a flat slab into a rounded leaf shape with notched edge.
Make a woodland bear or rabbit planter using the same bowl-plus-head construction.
Leave the frog unglazed with a natural clay finish for an earthy, unfussy look.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Head or legs fell off during drying
items.cause: The join was made when the bowl was already too dry for slip to bond
items.fix: Re-attach with fresh slip pressed into scored surfaces. If bone-dry, use strong PVA adhesive. Support the head with a prop while drying

items.cause: Coils added when the base had dried too much, creating a rigid-to-flexible join
items.fix: Keep the base under a cloth while coil-building to maintain matching moisture levels across all pieces
